passages.title: A Village in Mourning
passages.text:
When Mrs Hanh's husband **died** in a road accident, the whole village was shocked. The **tragedy** left her a **widow** at the age of forty, and for months she felt **miserable**. She could not eat, and the sadness seemed to **linger** in the house like a heavy smell.

Then a **dispute** over the family's land began with her brother-in-law. Everyone feared it would end in court. Fortunately, the two of them used to **get on well with** each other before the accident, so the neighbours persuaded them to sit down and talk. After three long meetings, they agreed to share the land equally.

Hanh was surprised by how much better she felt. Although her husband was **dead**, his memory stayed **alive** in the stories her children told every evening. Slowly, she began to smile again.
passages.summary_vi: Sau cái chết của chồng, bà Hạnh đau khổ nhưng dần vượt qua nhờ giải quyết tranh chấp đất và nhờ ký ức về chồng.

passages.title: My Uncle's Second Chance
passages.text:
My uncle Minh is a **middle-aged** man with an interesting story. He first **got married** at twenty-five, but he and his wife **got divorced** after only four years. For a long time he lived alone and said he would never **get married to** anyone again.

Then he met a kind teacher called Lan and, in 2019, he **married** her at a quiet family dinner. Lan's parents liked him at once, and he **got on with** her whole family from the first day.

Now they have a **toddler**, a boy called Bao, who spends the whole day **toddling** around the garden and picking up leaves. Everyone in our family agrees that my uncle looks happier than ever. He says that the unhappy years taught him how to be a better husband and father.

passages.title: The Residents of Willow Street
passages.text:
A local student interviewed people on Willow Street for a school project. The street has **approximately** two hundred residents, and **roughly** half of them are families with children. The youngest parents are **in their early thirties**, while the oldest neighbour is **nearly** ninety. In fact, Mr Tam will be ninety next month.

Mrs Linh, who is **in her mid-forties**, **brought up** four children on her own. She is **strict** about homework and bedtime, but her children say she is also very kind. Her neighbour, Mr Hoa, is **in his late fifties** and has just retired. He enjoys telling the younger families stories about how the street looked fifty years ago.

The student concluded that Willow Street is a friendly place where every generation helps the others. Every New Year, the whole street gathers for a long dinner outside, and nobody ever goes home hungry.

passages.title: Cousin Duc's Weekend Visit
passages.text:
Last Saturday my cousin Duc **came around** to talk about his problems at home. His parents are careful: they do not **allow him to** go out on school nights. At weekends he **is allowed to** visit friends, but he must be back early, so he rarely gets to **stay out late**.

He complained for an hour, until I noticed he **has got** ink on his shirt from his pen. "You should **get on with** your homework instead of worrying," I joked.

Duc laughed. He admitted that he had **managed to** pass his last maths test only because his mother helped him. Maybe, I said, it was time to **manage** his own time and money. By the evening he looked calmer, and we cooked dinner together. Before he left, he thanked me and promised to come back again next weekend with his guitar.

passages.title: Mai's Love Story
passages.text:
Mai remembers her first **date** very clearly. Khoa, a boy from her English class, **took her to** a small café by the river. She was so nervous that she spilled her tea.

Mai **went out with** Khoa for **a couple of** years. Slowly they **got to know** each other's habits and dreams, and she realised she was **in love**. But then Khoa moved to another city for work, and they **broke up**. Mai was sad for months and stayed at home reading novels.

Eventually she met Tuan, a gentle doctor who loved cooking. Within a year she **got engaged to** him. Mai says that her first heartbreak was painful, but it prepared her for a stronger relationship. Today she often tells her younger sister that patience and honesty are the keys to happiness, and that it is always safe to trust your heart after some time has passed.

passages.title: My Parents' Wedding Day
passages.text:
My parents' wedding **ceremony** took place in a garden in Hue. About eighty guests watched them exchange rings under a flower arch. **Afterwards**, everyone moved to a big tent for the **reception**, where there was delicious food, live music and a lot of dancing. The **celebration** lasted until midnight.

The next morning the couple **went on honeymoon** to a quiet beach for ten days. They had a peaceful first year together, and in **the following year** my mother **got pregnant** with my older sister.

Every year, on their wedding **anniversary**, they return to the same garden and have lunch under the same tree. My father always brings a single red rose. I hope that one day I will have a love story as warm as theirs. My grandmother still keeps a photo album from that day, and she shows it to every visitor.

passages.title: A First-Aid Lesson
passages.text:
Last week our class had a first-aid lesson. The nurse began with a quick biology reminder: the **bladder** stores urine, while the **rectum** is the last part of the large intestine. Then she moved on to practical advice.

"Be careful not to **cut yourself** with a kitchen knife," she said. "A small wound will usually **bleed** for a few minutes. When it stops, **put a bandage around** the finger and keep it clean."

She added that if you have a headache that does not go away, you can **take some tablets**, but you must read the label first. If a child has a fever, you should **give him some medicine**, and always check the right amount. "If you **feel sick** after taking it, call a doctor immediately," she warned. We all took notes, because this advice could really save a life.

passages.title: Grandfather's Warning
passages.text:
My grandfather smoked for forty years. Last winter he began to **suffer from** a terrible cough, and his chest started to **ache** every night. At first he refused to **see a doctor**. Instead, he asked me to **go to the chemist** to buy cough medicine.

But the cough got worse, and even breathing became **painful**. "Where does it **hurt**?" the doctor asked at last. After several tests, she told us that he had **lung cancer**. He had to **go into hospital** for an operation.

The family was very afraid, because his brother had died of a **heart attack** at sixty. Fortunately, the operation went well. Grandfather has stopped smoking, and he now uses every family dinner to warn the young people about the dangers of cigarettes. He says that looking after your health is the greatest gift you can give your family.

passages.text:
When I started university, I had almost no savings, so I decided to **get a loan** from a **financial institution** near the campus. I had to **pay interest on** the loan every month, which made my budget even tighter. I also needed **one month's rent** as a deposit for my flat.

My father reminded me to **put money away for a rainy day**, and I tried to follow his advice. I also **owe my brother money**, because he paid for my textbooks. I promised to **pay back** every cent by the summer.

It was a hard year, but after working part-time **for a period of time**, I could finally open my bank app and see that my account was **in credit**. That small number on the screen made me feel proud and free.

passages.title: Behind the Fashion Show
passages.text:
Backstage at the fashion show, the models had only thirty minutes to **get dressed**. One young woman wore a white shirt with a high **collar** and long **sleeves**. Just before she went out, the designer noticed that a **button** was missing and sewed a new one on in seconds.

Then came the accessories. A soft silk **scarf** was tied around her neck, and she put on silver **earrings**. The designer added a gold **necklace** and a thin **bracelet** on her left wrist. "Accessories finish the story," he said.

The audience loved the collection, especially the way simple clothes became elegant with small details. Photographers took hundreds of pictures. Afterwards the young model told me that the hardest part was staying calm while everything happened so fast. It was a busy night, but the whole team was proud of the result.

passages.title: Bargain Hunting at the Market
passages.text:
Last Sunday I went to the night market with my sister. She wanted a jacket with a deep **pocket** for her phone, and she insisted that the **zip** must be strong. "It is **likely** that the first price is too high," she whispered, "so we must **haggle**."

The seller wanted two hundred thousand dong, but my sister decided to **haggle over the price** for ten minutes. Finally he agreed to a much lower price, because he **is likely to** lose a customer if he refuses.

Another stall had a special offer: **three for the price of two** on T-shirts. The sign was bright red and designed to **call attention to** the discount. I bought three shirts and felt like a winner. My sister smiled and said that bargaining is not rude; it is simply part of the fun of shopping.

passages.title: A Road Trip Through the Countryside
passages.text:
Last summer my uncle and I took a road trip through the northern mountains. The **scenery** was beautiful: rice terraces, green valleys and fields of golden **barley**. We stopped at a roadside market, where a woman was selling **raw meat** and fresh **prawns** from a nearby river. We bought only some fruit, because we did not have a fridge.

On a narrow mountain road, we saw a sign that said **no overtaking**, but a lorry driver ignored it. Suddenly a motorbike appeared, and the lorry nearly hit it. Two people **were injured**, though not seriously, and we helped them until an ambulance arrived.

Because of the accident we **ended up** in a small village for the night. The family who hosted us had a **work-related connection** with my uncle: they supplied tea to his company. It was a lucky ending to an unlucky day.

passages.title: Learning English the Smart Way
passages.text:
When Tan started learning English, he used to **look up** every new word in a dictionary, and the list grew longer every day. At school he studied **in up to ten subjects**, so he had little time, but he was determined. After secondary school, he joined a short course of **vocational training** in tourism, because he wanted to work with foreign guests.

His teacher told him that a student who **has a wide vocabulary** can express ideas clearly. So Tan began to **write an essay** every week and asked his teacher to check it **accurately**. Gradually he started to **become more fluent**.

Today Tan can speak **fluently** about food, travel and culture, and he is now a guide in Hoi An. He says the secret is simple: read a little, write a little, and practise every day.

passages.title: Why Is English So Tricky?
passages.text:
Students often ask me why English is so tricky. First, pronunciation is a challenge. If you **have a good accent**, people understand you more easily, and many learners **have problems with** difficult **consonants**, such as "th". They often **get things wrong** when the spelling and the sound are different.

However, there are also easy ways to improve. Some children simply **pick things up** by watching cartoons and listening to songs. Adults need more discipline. I tell my learners to listen to short podcasts every day, and **in particular** to copy the rhythm of the speakers.

Of course, you also need to **revise for** your tests, and you must **pass an exam** to get a certificate. But remember that mistakes are normal. Every mistake is a small step towards better English.

passages.title: Advice Before the Big Test
passages.text:
Dear students, the final test is only two weeks away, and I want to share some advice. If you want to **do well**, plan your time carefully. Every day, remember to **do your best**, even when you feel tired. Please **try your best** to finish the practice papers on time.

Every Sunday, **do some revision** of the vocabulary and grammar from the week. If you can, **do exam preparation** with a friend, because explaining answers to someone else helps you remember. In class, you will also need to **do an essay**, so practise writing a clear introduction and conclusion.

If you follow this plan, you will probably **get a good grade** in speaking and **get a good mark** in writing. Remember to sleep well and eat breakfast on the exam morning. I believe in you all.

passages.title: Cramming Is Not the Answer
passages.text:
Exams are stressful, and many students **find it difficult to** concentrate for long hours. Ms Thu, a teacher with fifteen years of experience, suggests a smarter way. First, break the syllabus into small parts so you can **get through** it step by step. Then give each part a goal.

"A bad **mark** is not the end of the world," she says. "A **grade** only shows your level on one day." She asks students to review their mistakes and plan their **revision** carefully. A long period of **exam preparation** is more effective than one frightened night.

Ms Thu also encourages students to **do biology** or another subject they love, because motivation matters. Success needs consistent work, and **with a bit of luck**, every student can improve. She smiles as she says it, and her students believe her.

passages.title: Three Dreams, Three Careers
passages.text:
At dinner last night, my three cousins talked about their future. Anh, the oldest, wants to study **medicine** because she dreams of being **a doctor** in a mountain hospital. Her brother Bao prefers **law**. He says that **a lawyer** helps people who cannot defend themselves, and he often watches courtroom films.

The youngest, Chi, is only sixteen, but she already has a plan. She loves maths and machines, so she wants to study **engineering** and become **an engineer** who designs bridges. "One day I will **become** a leader in my field," she said proudly.

My uncle listened quietly and smiled. His own dream was to **go into business**, but he never had the chance. "Choose what you love," he told them. "Money will follow if you work hard."

I realised that every family dinner can be a small career workshop.

passages.text:
Choosing a university subject is difficult, so I made a list of options. Linh loves drawing and design, so she wants to study **architecture** and one day be **an architect** who builds eco-friendly houses. Her friend Quang enjoys reading about banks and prices, so he chose **economics**. He dreams of working as **an economist** at a national bank.

Another friend, Hoa, is fascinated by feelings. She studies **psychology** and hopes to become **a psychologist** who helps teenagers with stress. Finally there is Minh, who is energetic and confident. He prefers **business studies**, and he wants to be **a businessman** with his own company.

I am still not sure which path to choose. But after listening to my friends, I understand one thing: the best subject is the one that makes you curious every morning.

passages.title: My Resolution About Memory
passages.text:
Last January, Nam **started the year with a resolution to** improve his memory. He read a short book which explained that memory has several parts, and the first **component** is called **sensory memory**. This system **takes in information from** the eyes and ears, but it keeps it for only a few seconds.

Then the information moves to a short-term **holding area**, where it waits to be processed. To **put information into** long-term memory, Nam learned, you must pay attention and repeat it. Once something is in the holding area, you can **transfer it into** long-term memory by reviewing it again and again.

"To **keep your resolution**," his teacher advised, "make a tiny plan and follow it every day." Nam now reviews ten new words each night before bed. After three months, he can remember almost everything he learns, and he feels much more confident at school.

passages.title: Smart Ways to Study
passages.text:
Professor Lee shared **key points for effective study** with first-year students. First, **make an effort to** start early, even if the exam is far away. Many students **cram** the night before a test, but this rarely works because the brain needs time to organise new information.

Instead, read one chapter, then **recite** the main ideas aloud without looking at the book. Look carefully at each **illustration** in the textbook, because pictures can explain complicated ideas better than long sentences.

After learning something new, **give it time to soak in**, for example by taking a short walk or having a snack. Finally, **work on** your weakest topic first, not the easiest one. "Small, steady steps beat last-minute panic," the professor told the class. The students wrote this sentence on the board and promised to follow it.

passages.title: The Party That Nearly Failed
passages.text:
On Saturday I organised a birthday party **on my own**, with no help from anyone. I cooked dinner, decorated the room and chose the music. At first everything looked perfect. But around ten o'clock, things began to **go wrong**: the speakers stopped working and the cake fell on the floor.

Fortunately, the guests simply laughed. When someone started a dance competition, the party began to **get wild**, and soon everyone was singing together. The neighbours came to see what was happening, and they brought snacks **as well**.

In the end, the evening was a great success because we enjoyed the problems instead of worrying about them. Next year I will ask a friend for help, but I will always remember that small disasters can create the best memories. My friends have already promised to help me plan another party for the spring.

passages.title: From a First Coffee to a Honeymoon
passages.text:
Tuan was shy, so it took him months to invite Hoa for a coffee. When she finally said yes, he decided to **take someone to** a quiet café by the river, a place he had always loved. They talked for hours, and over the following weeks they began to **get to know** each other's families, habits and dreams. Within a year they were happy to **go out with** each other openly, and their friends stopped teasing them.

Not every story is so smooth. Hoa's cousin dated a man for five years, but the two had to **break up** when he moved abroad. Hoa and Tuan were luckier. Two years later he asked her to **get engaged to** him on the same bench by the river, and the following summer they chose to **go on honeymoon** in Da Lat. Hoa laughed when her doctor said she was likely to **get pregnant** soon, because they had planned a quiet year. "Life never follows the plan," she told Tuan, "but I would not change this one."

passages.title: A Messy Saturday
passages.text:
On Saturday my friend Mai decided to **come around** and help me prepare for an English interview. She arrived late, because she had been painting her flat. "Sorry, I **have got paint on** my jacket," she said, pointing at the **sleeve**. She had also lost one **earring** in the mess, which made us both laugh.

"Let's **get on with** the practice," she said, and she opened her notebook. A good speaker, she explained, should **have a wide vocabulary**, because repeating the same simple words makes your answers sound weak. She also reminded me that it does not matter whether you **have a good accent** or not, as long as people can understand you.

Before leaving, she warned me about the old staircase outside my flat. "It is very easy to **be injured** there when the steps are wet," she said. I promised to be careful, and we agreed to meet again the following Saturday.
